docs.title: Machine learning, explained
docs.body:
Intelligence runs real machine learning on your own device: a bundled Python environment with scikit-learn reads your CSV, learns statistical patterns from a training portion of the rows, and is scored on a held-out test portion it never saw during training.

There are three families of tasks this workspace supports. **Classification** predicts a category — for example whether a gemstone is *premium* or *standard*, or whether a customer will return. **Regression** predicts a number — for example an estimated price in rupees for an ornament of a given weight and purity. **Clustering** has no target at all: the engine groups records that behave similarly (for example customer segments) and you name the groups afterwards.

How a model learns. An algorithm looks at your feature columns (the predictors) and the target column (the thing to predict - supervised tasks only). It adjusts internal parameters until its guesses on the training rows match the real target values as well as possible. Random Forest and Gradient Boosting grow many small decision trees and average/vote; Logistic and Linear models fit simple mathematical curves; K-Means iteratively moves group centres until records sit closer to their own centre than any other.

How honest the score is. Every metric you see in Intelligence is computed on **test rows the model never trained on**. That is the whole point: a student who sees the answer sheet in class will ace the exam, so we hold out 20-50% of rows (your choice in the training workflow) and only ever report performance on them. The train score is never shown as the test score.

When machine learning is the wrong tool. With fewer than ~30 rows, predictions are mostly memorisation and even honest scores are noisy. With duplicated columns that echo the target (leakage), scores look brilliant and are useless. With columns that are actually later information (recorded *after* the event you predict), the model is clairvoyant in training and blind in production. The workspace flags obvious cases; the dataset preparation guide explains the rest.

docs.title: Classification guide
docs.body:
Classification predicts which category a row belongs to. Pick it when your target column holds labels rather than quantities: premium/standard, pass/fail, customer/won't-return.

Setting up. Choose the column with the labels as the target. Everything else should be a genuine predictor available *before* the outcome was known. Auto mode trains five candidates on the same split and reports the best by macro F1:

- **Logistic Regression** - a weighted linear vote; coefficients stay readable (positive weight pushes toward the positive class). Robust on small data.
- **Random Forest** - 300 decorrelated decision trees voting. Handles categorical-ish and skewed features well and almost always beats the linear baseline.
- **Decision Tree** - a single if/else tree. Fully readable but overfits easily on small data - the honest test score will say so.
- **Gradient Boosting** - trees added sequentially to fix earlier errors. Usually the accuracy leader; slower to train.
- **Linear SVC** - a maximum-margin linear boundary. No class probabilities available from this learner.

Reading the results. **Accuracy** is the share of correct predictions but lies when classes are imbalanced (99% records and 1% misses will look great at 99% accuracy while never catching a miss). **Precision** of a class: when the model says this class, how often is it right. **Recall**: of the real cases of this class, how many were found. **F1** balances the two and is the ranking score used for model selection here (macro-averaged so rare classes count fairly). **ROC-AUC** (when class probabilities are available) summarises how well the model ranks a random positive above a random negative across thresholds; 0.5 is a coin flip, above 0.9 is a strong ranker, and it is unavailable for models that emit no probabilities - the UI will say so rather than invent a number.

The per-class report shows precision/recall/F1 for each label separately, so you can see when the model is systematically downgrading one group. The confusion matrix shows which labels get mistaken for which.

Cautions. Classes with fewer than a handful of rows produce unstable recall values. If every row carries a unique label-like column (an order ID), it is noise - unselect it. If accuracy sits exactly at the majority share, the model learned to only predict the most common class; try more informative features.

docs.title: Regression guide
docs.body:
Regression predicts a numeric quantity. Pick it when your target column holds numbers with meaningful magnitude: a price, a weight, a duration.

Setting up. Choose the numeric target column. Auto mode trains five candidates on the same split and reports the best by R²:

- **Linear Regression** - plain least squares; the coefficients are directly interpretable (rupees per gram of gold, roughly).
- **Ridge Regression** - least squares with an L2 penalty; better with correlated features and it shrinks wild coefficients.
- **Random Forest Regressor** - 300 trees averaging piecewise estimates; captures non-linear pricing (e.g. premium brand tiers) that linear models miss.
- **Decision Tree Regressor** - a single tree; stepwise estimates, easy to overfit.
- **Gradient Boosting Regressor** - sequential error-correcting trees; usually the accuracy leader.

Reading the results.
- **MAE** - mean absolute error, in the target's own units. "MAE 15,000 LKR" reads naturally.
- **MSE / RMSE** - squared and root-squared error; RMSE punishes big misses disproportionately and also reads in target units.
- **R²** - the share of target variance explained: 1.0 perfect, 0.0 no better than always predicting the mean, and negative means the model is genuinely worse than that baseline. A great R² with a huge RMSE just means the target is large-scaled - always read R² next to MAE/RMSE.

The actual-vs-predicted scatter should hug the diagonal. The residual chart (actual minus predicted) should look like an even scatter around zero with no curve and no funnel: a U-shape means the model is missing a non-linear term, a funnel means errors grow with size - common when prices are modelled linearly.

Cautions. Never present a regression prediction as a probability - this workspace deliberately does not. These learners do not estimate calibrated prediction intervals, so the prediction view shows the value (and the honest residual standard deviation as a rough dispersion hint for tree ensembles) and says plainly when no reliable interval is available. Watch for leakage columns such as a *final agreed price* when predicting *asking price*.

docs.title: Clustering guide
docs.body:
Clustering finds groups without any target column. Use it to explore: how do my customers or inventory items naturally divide?

Choose features that describe behaviour sensibly. Raw scales matter greatly - a column in rupees (0-100,000) will dominate a 1-10 rating unless it is scaled. Intelligence scales numeric features inside the pipeline automatically before clustering (and encodes categorical ones with one-hot), so the axes you see in the cluster map are standardised, not raw.

**K-Means** partitions rows into exactly K groups around moving centres. Choosing K is a judgement call: small Ks give broad strokes; when K grows much past 10 the map gets noisy. Between K should be 2-8 for most explorations. K-Means always reports an inertia - the within-group spread - but lower inertia by itself always favours more groups, so it is a tie-breaking number, not a verdict.

**DBSCAN** groups points by density and explicitly labels low-density stragglers as *noise* rather than forcing them into a group. It needs a neighbourhood radius (eps) on the standardised scale and a minimum group size (min_samples); Intelligence offers its defaults and shows the noise share honestly. If it says 40% noise, that is a real finding about your data's granularity, not a bug.

Reading the results. **Silhouette** (−1 to 1, reported whenever there are at least 2 groups with ≥2 members) measures how much better each point fits its own group than its nearest neighbouring group: above 0.5 is a clean, well-separated structure; 0.2-0.5 is a usable but fuzzy one; close to 0 or negative means the groups overlap and other features (or another K) should be tried. Silhouette is how the auto-comparison ranks candidates when it can; otherwise the first candidate is kept and the UI shows it plainly.

The cluster map projects every row to two dimensions so you can eyeball the shapes; groups are coloured and noise is grey. Cluster distances on the prediction view measure how far a new record sits from its assigned group centre - a useful confidence-ish signal for K-Means (smaller is more typical of that group).

Caution: clusters are descriptive, not ground truth. Name them by inspecting their members (the preview table sorted by cluster ID); `Group 2` is only meaningful once you decide what its rows have in common.

docs.title: Dataset preparation guide
docs.body:
Everything downstream inherits the quality of the CSV you import. Ten minutes of preparation is usually worth more than any algorithm choice.

One row, one fact. Each row should describe one record - one sale, one customer, one measurement. Avoid one giant row per month with dozens of product columns; those are hard for any model to read. Columns that exist only to identify rows (order ID, receipt number, row number) carry no predictive signal and add noise: unselect them in the training page (they are pre-deselected for you when the column name looks like an ID).

Missing values. The pipeline mean-imputes numeric columns, median-imputes for skewed ones, uses a constant

token for categorical ones, and handles date columns by year/month/day features. That is a reasonable default, but a column that is missing for a *reason* (a discount field that is blank exactly when no discount applied) may deserve its own explicit 'is set' flag column before import.

Duplicates and mistakes. Import reports duplicate-row counts and the preview's search helps find repeated rows. Exact duplicates can double-weight a line of evidence. Encoding is detected (UTF-8 native, common single-byte fallbacks) and delimiters (comma/semicolon/tab) are sniffed automatically; see the CSV troubleshooting guide when a column lands looking strange.

Dates. ISO-style dates (2026-03-14 or 2026-03-14 09:30) parse automatically. Ambiguous formats like 03/04/2026 are risky - the partition rule (day-first vs month-first) differs by country. Convert to ISO format before import for unambiguous features such as *days since*.

Targets and leakage. The chosen target must exist in the CSV, and columns that echo it must be excluded from the features. Classic leakage: predicting final price while including agreed-price, or predicting churn while including *active* flag (which is the outcome itself). The training page blocks selecting the target as a feature, and features whose value distribution is nearly identical to the target are flagged.

Scale and coverage. As a rule of thumb aim for at least ~30 rows per expected class or cluster before trusting evaluation metrics; below that the workspace will warn you that limits are too small for reliable estimation rather than show impressive-but-meaningless numbers.

docs.title: Metrics reference
docs.body:
Every number here is computed on the held-out test rows only. A quick reference for reading each one honestly.

**Classification**
- Accuracy - share of test rows predicted correctly. Treat with suspicion under class imbalance.
- Precision (per class) - of rows predicted as this class, the share that were right. High precision matters when a false alarm is expensive.
- Recall (per class, sometimes called sensitivity) - of the real cases of this class, the share that were found. High recall matters when a missed case is expensive.
- F1 (macro) - the harmonic balance of precision/recall, averaged over classes with equal weight. This is the score ranking candidates in classification comparison.
- ROC-AUC - the probability the model ranks a random positive above a random negative. Computed for binary tasks with class probabilities (OvR macro-mean for multiclass). Not defined for learners without probabilities - shown as unavailable, never estimated.
- Confusion matrix - the count of each actual-vs-predicted pair; the diagonal is correct.

**Regression**
- MAE - average absolute miss, in target units.
- MSE - average squared miss; scale-sensitive and dominated by large misses.
- RMSE - the root of MSE, back in target units; comparable against MAE when you ask "how bad are the worst misses".
- R² - fraction of target variance explained. Read alongside error magnitudes, never in isolation.
- Residual mean/std - systematic bias and typical dispersion of misses. A mean far from zero means the model over- or under-predicts on average.

**Clustering**
- Silhouette - (mean over rows) how well each row fits its own group versus the nearest other group; −1 .. 1. Reported only when structurally valid, otherwise shown as unavailable.
- Cluster sizes - per-group member counts; wildly lopsided sizes often mean the K was higher than the data's real structure.
- Inertia (K-Means only) - within-group squared spread. Lower is tighter, but it improves monotonically with more groups, so it never selects K by itself.
- Noise count/share (DBSCAN) - rows too isolated to belong to any group; reported exactly as found.

**Why visible scores can be small or absent.** Evaluation is only as reliable as the test portion; with fewer than roughly 20 held-out rows the workspace prints a size warning beside the metrics rather than pretending precision. Confidence percentages appear on the prediction view only for classification models that produce real class probabilities; for regression and clustering they do not exist and are not faked.

docs.title: Model selection guide
docs.body:
How to pick sensibly rather than chase the top score.

**Start from the task, not the algorithm.** Classification for labels, regression for quantities, clustering for unlabelled exploration. Then decide what mistake costs more: false alarms (favour precision) or missed cases (favour recall). The ranking score in classification is macro-F1 because it balances both without letting the majority class dominate.

**Use the comparison table.** "Compare candidates" trains every algorithm for the task on one identical split and reports each one's score, duration and any failure reason. The table only compares like with like - algorithms for different tasks are never scored against each other, because accuracy and R² are on different scales.

**Small margins are not evidence.** Between two Random-Forest-style candidates 0.974 versus 0.971 is noise on a few hundred test rows. Prefer the simpler, faster, more interpretable model unless the gap is real and repeatable (try a different random seed or split to confirm).

**Bigger wins on tiny data are usually frail.** Gradient Boosting snatching a large lead on a 60-row dataset often means it memorised directions that don't generalise; a linear model in second place is the safer deploy. The library shows train/test row counts with every model so this trade-off stays visible.

**Speed counts at prediction time.** The duration column distinguishes 0.2s from 45s training, and that gap repeats at every future prediction run on the same scale. For repeated batch predictions, a 0.001 difference in score rarely justifies a 50× runtime.

**Keep the winner's full provenance.** Every saved model stores its algorithm, feature list, test split, seed, checksum and held-out metrics in the library - rename it meaningfully ("gold price GBM · march") so you can pick it out later. Model files are version-checked against the checksum at every prediction run and the run is refused if the file has changed.

docs.title: CSV troubleshooting
docs.body:
Import behaves like a resilient CSV reader: it sniffs delimiters (comma, semicolon, tab), encoding (UTF-8 first, common single-byte fallbacks after), header presence, and robust quote handling. But real files lie about being tables. Fixes for the usual suspects:

**Many columns merged into one.** The delimiter inside the file is not the one that was detected. The ingest auto-detects comma/semicolon/tab per file; when a strange delimiter remains, open the file in a text editor and confirm which character separates fields on a data line.

**Numbers arrive as text (or "categorical").** The type detector samples rows and falls back to categorical when the numeric share is low. Common causes: thousands separators with commas inside a comma-CSV ("1,250"), currency symbols, trailing spaces, or mixed units in one column. Clean to plain digits before import.

**Dates parsed inconsistently.** Ambiguous dd/mm vs mm/dd ordering is the usual reason. Re-export ambiguous columns in ISO (YYYY-MM-DD).

**Blank values everywhere.** Empty strings, bare "-", "N/A", "NULL" are treated as missing and counted in the missing-value statistics. Real values spelled as any of those strings cannot be distinguished and become missing - rename them ("none") before import if they are meaningful.

**The first column appears named oddly.** The file probably has an Excel BOM or a title row above the header. Remove the title row; the header detection expects the first row to be the column names.

**Encoding garbage characters (Ã©, â€™).** The file is UTF-8 that was re-encoded wrongly upstream (opened in a non-UTF-8 editor and re-saved). Re-download the original or re-export with UTF-8 encoding.

**Huge file (>512 MB).** Import is capped at 512 MB and 2,000,000 rows so the preview and training stay responsive. Split the file, or reduce columns before importing.

**Still broken?** Import reports zero rows → the file has a header but no data rows; values "no data available" → check the file has at least one data row below the header. Export a copy of what got imported (dataset page → Export copy) to see exactly how the engine read your file.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.body:
**Feature** - a predictor column the model reads.
**Target** - the column being predicted (supervised tasks only).
**Row / record** - one line of the dataset, one observation.
**Train set** - the portion of rows the model learns from.
**Test set** - the held-out portion used only for honest evaluation; never part of training.
**Test split** - the fraction of rows reserved for testing (20-50% here).
**Pipeline** - the saved chain of preprocessing (imputation, encoding, scaling) plus the model; prediction always re-applies exactly what training used.
**Imputation** - filling missing values with computed stand-ins (mean/median/constant token).
**Encoding (one-hot)** - turning a category column into one 0/1 column per possible value.
**Scaling** - putting numeric columns on comparable ranges so no one column dominates by being counted in bigger units.
**Leakage** - when a feature secretly contains information about the target; inflates scores that will not replicate.
**Overfitting** - the model memorising training rows rather than learning a general pattern; visible when test scores collapse relative to expectations.
**Hyperparameter** - a setting chosen before learning (number of trees, K clusters, seed) rather than fitted.
**Seed / random state** - the fixed shuffling randomness so a run can be reproduced exactly.
**Class balance** - how evenly rows distribute across target categories; imbalance makes accuracy misleading.
**Macro average** - averaging per-class scores with equal weight, so rare classes count as much as common ones.
**Silhouette** - cluster quality measure: how much better each row fits its own group than its nearest other group.
**Inertia** - K-Means's within-group spread; lower is tighter but never selects K alone.
**ROC-AUC** - ranking quality of a classification model across thresholds.
**Confusion matrix** - table of actual-vs-predicted counts per class.
**Residual** - actual value minus predicted value for one row.
**Checkpoint / bundle version** - the internal format version of a saved model file; stored so invalid or outdated files are detected before being used.
